title: An hour without the phone

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shabbat, from a Hebrew root for stopping. Your line was a day off from making. When is your rest window this week? Day one hundred forty-four.

Quick test. Where's your phone right now? If you're listening to this, probably in your hand. Fair enough. But think about the rest of the day. On the table at dinner. On the pillow at night. In your pocket on a walk, buzzing against your leg, or not buzzing, and you check anyway. A whole day off, like the Sabbath we met yesterday, can sound impossible from here. So we're not starting with a day. We're starting with sixty minutes, and a piece of furniture. Today's practice is an hour without the phone.
screen: `WHERE'S YOUR PHONE?` → `NOT A DAY. AN HOUR.` → `AN HOUR WITHOUT THE PHONE.`

segments.voice: Here's a surprising finding. In a 2017 study at the University of Texas, people did tests of attention and memory with their phone in one of three places: on the desk, face down; in a pocket or bag; or in another room. Phones were silent the whole time. The people whose phones were in another room did best. The researchers called the effect brain drain: part of your mind stays busy not checking the phone. Later studies have found smaller or mixed effects, so hold it loosely. But the lesson most people recognize from their own lives is simple. Face down isn't away. Silent isn't away. Away is away. That's why the practice has a drawer in it. Out of sight works better than willpower, because you're not spending the hour resisting. You've just made it a little harder to reach. There's a modern movement that took this straight from the Sabbath. In 2010, a Jewish nonprofit started a National Day of Unplugging, and writers and families since have kept what some call a tech sabbath: one day a week without screens. That's the destination this week. But nearly everyone who does it says the same thing: start smaller than you think. One hour. Pick one that's easy, like a walk or cooking dinner. Put the phone in a drawer, or another room, and close it. You'll probably reach for your pocket a few times. That's the habit showing itself. Let the hand come back empty.
screen: `THREE PLACES FOR THE PHONE.` · `FACE DOWN ISN'T AWAY.` · `A TECH SABBATH.` · `START WITH ONE HOUR.` · then, large: `THE DRAWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rehearse your hour. When this session ends, notice where your phone will go. For now, settle, and breathe. Picture the drawer, or the other room. Picture sliding the phone in and closing it. Notice what your body does: a small tightening, maybe, or relief. Now picture the hour itself, the room quiet, your hands free. Choose which hour today it will be. The bell holds the time.
An hour without the phone. Not face down, not silent: out of sight, for sixty minutes, the first step toward a weekly rest. Today's word.
screen: `AN HOUR WITHOUT THE PHONE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the drawer. Today, put your phone in a drawer, or another room, for one hour. When your hand reaches for it, let it come back empty. Day one hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: People who keep a tech sabbath often start with one screen-free hour, putting the phone in a drawer or another room, and lengthen it over weeks toward an evening or a full day.
